title: Ignoring the Wisdom of Crowds: why votes work for facts but veto innovation
summary: Jason Cohen explains why crowds are brilliant at estimating facts (jelly beans, Millionaire audience polls) because random errors cancel out. The same mechanism ruins creative work, where votes act as vetoes that leave bland, lowest-common-denominator output. Startups need a niche they can own, not a safe middle.

principles.text: Crowds are wise only when there is an objectively correct answer and individual errors cancel out.
principles.quote: There is "wisdom in the crowd" when there is an objectively-correct answer, and when the errors cancel out

principles.text: A small group that knows the answer can dominate a poll because ignorant voters cancel each other out.
principles.quote: The ignorant people vote randomly and *their votes cancel out*, leaving the few in control of the result.

principles.text: In creative work, votes are vetoes: consensus settles on what everyone hated least, not on something wonderful.
principles.quote: Votes don't converge on something wonderful. Rather, votes are *vetoes*.

principles.text: Design by committee strips out the interesting edges and leaves a boring residue, so great products aren't made that way.
principles.quote: In creative work, votes eliminate the interesting edges**, because votes result in subtracting rather than adding

principles.text: Startups should own a niche completely rather than occupy a gray middle that offends no one and excites no one.
principles.quote: Little companies need a niche--a market space they can completely, unquestionably own, not some gray middle-ground where your attempt to offend no one also means exciting no one.

principles.text: Building average products for the average consumer is the opposite of innovation and likely a bad product strategy.
principles.quote: design-by-committee is the antithesis of innovation.
